summary: Presents theoretical and practical reasons to redesign the ARPANET communication protocols. It discusses multipacket messages, Host retransmission, duplicate detection, sequencing and acknowledgment, and proposes simplifications to the IMP-to-IMP protocol.

eli5.summary: The author thinks the rules the network boxes follow are too complicated and suggests simpler ones.

subtitle: A critical analysis of ARPANET protocol design proposing simplifications

tldr.problem: ARPANET's host-to-host protocol achieves less than 40 kb/sec throughput on a single connection due to message-at-a-time transmission, and its message reassembly design creates potential lockup conditions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes moving message ordering, sequencing, retransmission, and duplicate detection from the network layer to the host layer, eliminating multipacket message reassembly and allowing hosts to send arbitrary-length messages split into single packets.
tldr.outcome: The analysis influenced later protocol designs, particularly showing the advantage of end-to-end responsibility for reliability—a principle that shaped TCP/IP and remains fundamental to modern networking.

today: RFC 635 is a foundational analysis that directly influenced the design of TCP, whose end-to-end acknowledgment, sequence numbering, and sliding window flow control reflect Cerf's insights here. Modern protocols across the internet owe a debt to this protocol critique.

sections.title: The Throughput Problem
sections.content:
RFC 635, written by Vinton Cerf, identifies a critical performance limitation in the ARPANET Host-to-Host protocol. Although the IMP subnet can theoretically deliver 80 kb/sec between hosts, the protocol itself allows only one message outstanding on a connection at a time, waiting for a Response From Next Message (RFNM) before the next message can be sent. This creates a bottleneck: as the number of hops increases, the throughput drops dramatically. For a 32-bit host sending across multiple hops, achievable throughput is limited to far less than the 40 kb/sec ceiling mentioned in early experiments.

The RFC analyzes this mathematically, showing that the message-at-a-time design creates a waiting period of h+m-1 packet times, where h is the number of hops and m is the number of packets per message.
sections.eli5: The protocol makes computers wait for a yes-signal after sending one message before sending the next. This wastes time, especially when computers are far apart.

sections.title: Core Design Problems
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several interconnected issues with current ARPANET design. Multipacket messages were created to send longer data in one unit, but they cause the destination IMP to reserve reassembly buffer space, which can lock up if too many messages arrive simultaneously. The IMP also orders messages for delivery, which paradoxically creates the same lockup problem: if the IMP holds out-of-order packets waiting to reorder them, it can run out of buffer space and deadlock.

Hosts cannot reliably retransmit lost messages because they cannot detect if a message was duplicated in transit. The current Host-to-Host protocol provides no end-to-end acknowledgment, relying instead on the RFNM—which signals only that the destination IMP accepted the message, not that the destination host received it.
sections.eli5: The system tries to do too much at once: ordering messages, reassembling packets, and managing buffers. This can cause it to jam up.

sections.title: Proposed Simplifications
sections.content:
Cerf proposes moving responsibilities from the network to the hosts. First, eliminate multipacket messages and IMP reassembly: hosts should split long data into single packets, and the IMP forwards packets without reordering them. Hosts handle sequencing, duplicate detection, and retransmission themselves. Second, introduce end-to-end acknowledgment at the host level, where the destination host explicitly confirms receipt, allowing the source host to reliably retransmit lost packets. Third, replace the simplex connections (separate one-way connections in each direction) with full-duplex connections, where acknowledgments and flow control information travel on the reverse path of the data stream.

The RFC also proposes using a sliding window for flow control, inspired by the French CYCLADES network, where the receiver grants permission to send a range of sequence numbers, allowing multiple packets in flight without deadlock risk.
sections.eli5: Let hosts do the hard work: keep track of which packets were received, ask to resend lost ones, and tell the sender how much it can send at once.
